terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, transitive: aliquem ad cēnam, in hospitium, domum invītāre
evidence: Cic. Off. 3.59: invītat Canius postrīdiē familiārēs suōs
terms.comment: The general word, with ad or in and the accusative, with domum, or with ut and the subjunctive (Cic. Att. 13.2, Lewis & Short). Things invite too, “tempt, attract” (Lucr. 5.524). Not to be confused with invītus, “unwilling”.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, transitive: ad cēnam vocāre
terms.comment: Its first sense is “call, summon”; asking someone to a meal was simply vocāre, and the invited guest is vocātus (Lewis & Short, s.v. vocō, “to bid, invite one as a guest”).

evidence: Cic. Att. 9.12.1: in Ēpīrum invītātiō quam suāvis! (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: Pompōnia, inquit, tū invītā mulierēs, ego virōs accīverō
phrases.english: “Pomponia,” he said, “you invite the women, and I’ll have fetched the men.”
the next day Canius invites his friends

phrases.latin: Quam vellem Menedēmum invītātum ut nōbīscum esset hodiē amplius
phrases.english: How I wish Menedemus had been invited, to be with us today as well

sources: Lewis & Short: invito · Lewis & Short: voco · Lewis & Short: invitatio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 334.
